title: Reading Input with cin
description: Asking a question and storing whatever the person types.

content.value: Until now every value was typed into the code before it ran. `cin` (say "see-in") reads what a person types at the keyboard, so the same program can give a different answer each time.

steps.label: Keyboard
steps.detail: The person types and presses Enter

steps.label: cin
steps.detail: C++'s name for the keyboard input

steps.label: Variable
steps.detail: The answer is stored for you to use

content.title: From your fingers to a variable
content.caption: `cin` lives in `<iostream>`, the same header that gives you `cout`.
Sample run: the program stops at the question and waits. Type `14`, press Enter, and it prints `Next year you will be 15`. The question has no `endl`, so you type your answer right next to it.

parts.label: variable
parts.note: Must already exist. Its type decides what is read.

content.title: Reading into a variable
content.caption: The arrows show the way the value travels: out of `cin`, into `age`.

items.sub: Declare the variable before you read into it. `cin` needs somewhere to put the answer.
It reads up to the Enter key, turns the characters into an `int`, and stores them.
`cout <<` sends a value out to the screen. `cin >>` pulls a value in.

content.question: Which line reads a number into `score`?
content.explain: `cin` comes first and the arrows point into the variable: `cin >> score;`.

content.title: cin reads to match the variable's type

steps.note: Make three empty variables, one of each type.
Ask. Suppose you type `14` and press Enter.
`age` is an `int`, so `cin` reads a whole number.

out: How tall are you, in metres? 1.6

steps.note: `height` is a `double`, so a decimal is read.

out: First letter of your name? M

content.title: One sample run
content.outro: Because `age` really is an `int`, `age + 1` would be arithmetic. With a `string`, `age + 1` would not even compile.

content.caption: Chain the arrows to read several values: `cin >> a >> b;`. `cin` skips spaces and Enters between values, so `3 4` on one line or on two lines both print `Their sum is 7`.

content.value: Type letters where `cin` expects a number and the read fails: the variable gets 0 and every later `cin` is skipped. Checking input needs decisions, which is the next module.

items.title: cin >> name
items.text: Stops at the first space. The rest waits in the queue for the next read.

items.title: getline(cin, name)
items.text: Reads the whole line up to Enter, spaces and all. Needs `<string>`.

content.caption: Sample run: type `Amara Okafor` and it prints `Hello, Amara Okafor!`. Pick the one that fits the question: a first name is a word, a full address is a line.

content.question: You type `New Delhi` for `cin >> city;` (a `string`). What is stored in `city`?
content.explain: `cin >>` stops at the first space. Only `getline` would keep the whole line.

content.value: `cin >> age` reads the digits and stops. The invisible Enter is left waiting. The next `getline` finds it and hands you an empty string without waiting at all.

steps.label: getline
steps.detail: Sees the Enter at once: name is `""`

content.title: Where the Enter goes
content.caption: The person typed `14` then Enter. Only the digits were taken.

items.title: Throw the Enter away
items.text: `cin.ignore()` skips exactly one character: the leftover Enter.

items.title: Lines first
items.text: Ask `getline` questions before number ones. The projects in this course do this.

content.caption: A third way: read every answer as a line, then convert with Module 2's `stoi` (or `stod` for a `double`). Type `3` and it prints `That will be 750 rupees.` No leftover Enter can cause trouble.

content.question: You type `14` for `cin >> age;`. What does the very next `getline(cin, name);` store?
content.explain: The leftover Enter is still in the queue, so `getline` stops at once with nothing in it.

practice.question: Ask for a favourite colour and print: Nice, <colour> is a good choice. Use `getline` so that two-word colours like sky blue work too.
Ask for two whole numbers with `cin >>` and print their sum.
Run this and watch the Name question get skipped. Then fix it by adding one `cin.ignore();` in the right place.

quiz.question: A `string` called `name` is read with `cin >> name;` and the person types `Amara Okafor`. What does `name` hold?
options: Amara, because `>>` stops at the first space
Nothing, because a space is not allowed
quiz.explain: `cin >>` reads one word. To keep the spaces, read the whole line with `getline(cin, name);`.

quiz.question: Why leave `endl` off the end of a question?
options: The cursor stays on the same line, so the answer is typed next to the question.
quiz.explain: Without `endl` the cursor stays where it is. With it, the person types their answer on the line below, which looks wrong.

quiz.question: Which line reads a whole line of text, spaces included, into a `string` called `line`?
quiz.explain: `getline` reads everything up to the Enter key. `cin >> line` stops at the first space, and `cin << line` does not compile because the arrows point the wrong way.

quiz.question: Why does a `getline` straight after a `cin >> age;` come back empty?
options: `getline` can only be used once per program.
`cin >>` leaves the Enter key in the queue, and `getline` reads up to it.
quiz.explain: `cin >> age` takes the digits but not the Enter that follows them. The next `getline` finds that leftover Enter and decides the line has already ended.

quiz.question: What is the simplest way to avoid that trap?
options: Ask the `getline` questions before the `cin >>` questions.
quiz.explain: The problem only happens when a `getline` follows a `cin >>`. Reordering the questions, or adding `cin.ignore();` to throw away the Enter, both fix it.
